extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, logic, and the foundations of science
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the epistemic status and evidential basis of axioms, definitions, and demonstrations in deductive sciences (geometry, arithmetic, mechanics) with attention to their inductive/hypothetical character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms as inductions from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms are generalizations from experience rather than truths known independently of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text asserts that 'axioms are but a class, the highest class, of inductions from experience' and that they 'rest upon superabundant and obvious evidence.' It insists the burden of proof lies on those who claim any other origin for axioms; examples and authorities are cited to support that axioms carry their inductive origin 'on the face of their enunciation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions are generalized, not strictly true
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions (in the geometrical sense) are generalizations from experience that assert some observed properties while (fictitiously) denying others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions are described as 'not even, accurately speaking, truths; being propositions in which, while we assert of some kind of object some property or properties which observation shows to belong to it, we at the same time deny that it possesses any other properties' — a denial made for convenience to exclude modifying circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive sciences are essentially inductive and hypothetical
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive or demonstrative sciences proceed by tracing consequences of assumptions but their evidence ultimately depends on observation and induction; their conclusions are conditional on the truth (or approximation to truth) of their premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter concludes 'Deductive or Demonstrative Sciences are all, without exception, Inductive Sciences' and argues their 'method ... is hypothetical' — one must determine how close the assumptions are to truth, often by observation repeated in each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of demonstrative results depends on premises' truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Results of deductive sciences are necessary only in the sense of following from axioms and definitions; their claim to necessity beyond that depends on establishing those first principles empirically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author states the results 'are indeed necessary, in the sense of necessarily following from certain first principles ... but their claim to the character of necessity ... must depend upon the previous establishment of such a claim in favour of the definitions and axioms themselves.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical/arithmetic truths rest on sensory evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental arithmetical truths (e.g., 'two and one are three') are grounded in sensory experience — counting physical objects — and are learned via the evidence of the senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes teaching numbers 'through the evidence of the senses' (apples, marbles) and argues that arithmetic's basic propositions are 'proved by showing to our eyes and our fingers' arrangements of objects; thus number-concepts and their axioms are inductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebra and arithmetic disguise induction via generality of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent purely verbal or nominal character of arithmetic/algebra is deceptive because the operations presuppose inductive inferences about 'numbers of something'; the generality of symbols conceals the fact that each algebraic step is an inference about things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although symbols (a, b, x) may not excite particular images, 'there is in every step of an arithmetical or algebraical calculation a real induction, a real inference of facts from facts.' The comprehensive nature of the generalization and mechanical habit of manipulation disguise the induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic's axioms: sums/differences of equals
rubrics_metrics.description: Arithmetic relies on two primary axioms: 'The sums of equals are equal' and 'The differences of equals are equal,' from which other propositions (including those about unequals via reductio ad absurdum) are derived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These axioms, like the so-called definitions, 'are results of induction; true of all objects whatever' though an investigation reveals hypothetical elements in their application (see units/equality concerns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical certainty conditional on unit-equivalence assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical certainty (unconditional truth and perfect accuracy) applies only when units are equivalent — the implicit assumption that '1 = 1' (i.e., all units are of the same kind) must hold, otherwise arithmetic conclusions may fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter warns that if units differ (e.g., troy vs avoirdupois pounds), arithmetic inferences about equality may not hold. Only when number is considered abstracted from other qualities does mathematical certainty properly apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish definitions that assert existence from mere verbal definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some 'definitions' (geometrical/arithmetic) assert not merely meanings of terms but the existence of objects meeting those descriptions; calculations depend on those existence-claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: calling 'Three is two and one' a definition is permissible only if one also accepts the arithmetical theorem that such collections (parcels/figures) exist; thus definitions in this sense carry empirical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate demonstrative arguments by separating (a) inference-from-assumptions and (b) truth-of-assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper method is to (1) perform, once for all, the logical tracing of consequences from assumptions (demonstrative part) and (2) separately examine, often by observation, how nearly the assumptions correspond to reality for each concrete case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains that 'the inquiry into the inferences which can be drawn from assumptions ... properly constitutes Demonstrative Science,' while whether the assumptions are true 'is generally a matter of observation, to be repeated in every fresh case.' This separation guides how to assess applicability and certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware assuming universal homogeneity without empirical support
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that certain properties (e.g., homogeneity of parts of distance, time, force) are self-evident are mistaken; their plausibility derives from repeated experience, not a priori insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Through examples (geometrical straightness, lever mechanics) the text argues that what seems 'self-evident' is often grounded in habitual experience; one cannot propose contrary imaginary cases intelligibly without relying on past experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess scope of general propositions: they must be verified across instances
rubrics_metrics.description: A necessary and universal truth relative to any object must 'verify itself in every instance' where that object is contemplated; simple and intelligible truths will be continually suggested by experience and command implicit assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer-quotation argues that universal axioms 'pervade all the objects of experience' and their continual suggestion by experience ensures their acceptance — thus when evaluating general propositions check their persistent, uncontradicted iteration in experience.
